## Introduction

Recent research on language variability has demonstrated how different language environments shape language and cognitive processes. Specifically, Heritage bilinguals offer a powerful lens for understanding how becoming a dominant speaker in the second acquired language despite not having the first years of development in the language can provide insights into the plasticity of the language system. Therefore, understanding how language processing is shaped by the heritage bilingual experience and how that may differ from monolingual or second language learner is an important gap to address in the bilingualism literature. 

For this project proposal, I would like to further explore heritage speakers of Spanish abilities to comprehend relative clauses across varying syntactic complexity. Therefore, in order to test, I will be replicating Fuchs and colleagues (2026)’s paper where they compared heritage speakers to English-raised bilinguals who are late bilinguals and learned Spanish only in the classroom setting and Spanish-raised bilinguals who were raised in Spanish-speaking dominant environment. They tested participants’ constraints when cognitive loading increased alongside syntactic complexity but also tested cognitive effort and syntactic complexity separately. For the purpose of this class, I will be replicating the experiment with heritage speakers in the picture-matching experiment which tested syntactic competence. The paper looked at three different types of sentences: Reduced Relative (RR), Subject Relative (SR), Object Relative (OR) in Spanish. RR tends to be the easiest condition as it follows a direct order of events for example “the bear painting the tiger.” SR on the other hand is when the subject becomes the actor so instead it is “the bear that is painting the tiger.” Finally, OR which is the most difficult syntactically as it starts with the noun where the sentence instead states “the bear that the tiger paints.” In this sentence, it is typically harder for people as they often initially assume the bear is the one enacting the painting and not the tiger but then have to revise their interpretation once they hear the full sentence. The key findings of this experiment is that for heritage speakers showed higher accuracy for Reduced Relatives than Subject Relatives (β = 0.87, SE = 0.22, z = 3.86, p < .001) and significantly higher accuracy for Subject Relatives than Object Relatives (β = 5.07, SE = 0.17, z = 29.52, p < .001), This means that heritage speakers tend to have difficulties in interpreting object relative clauses and show a relative-clause complexity effect. 


## Methods

To conduct this experiment, I will be implementing the experimental design from Fuchs and colleagues' (2026) design. Participants will hear a short Spanish phrase containing a relative clause and are instructed to select the picture that correctly matches the described event. Each trial will display two images depicting reversed agent-patient roles (e.g., a bear painting a tiger vs. a tiger painting a bear). The auditory stimuli will follow the structure of Article + Nouns + Relative Clause. As the task progresses, syntactic complexity will increase by using three types of relative clauses: Reduced Relatives, Subject Relative, and Object Relatives. All materials for this experiment has been provided through the OSF repository: https://osf.io/etprk/files/osfstorage?view_only=19f67921b4eb4ab58299685068ac0a16 along with analysis materials ensuring better replication of the experiment. 


The paper recruited 31 heritage Spanish speakers, who were born and raised in the U.S. or immigrated by age 6 and reported speaking Spanish with one or both parents. They also report English to be their most dominant language but having acquired Spanish since birth. Ensuring that I am recruiting the correct population and including the same criteria as the researchers will be the most important and challenging part of the project. This is because it will restrict the availability of people I can recruit from SONA but will be the most fitting to what the study tested. Additionally, the organization and coding of the experiment on JavaScript will also be another learning challenge since participants completed 120 picture-matching trials so it is a substantive amount of images and audios to be coded.
